text: Around 31% of women reported knowing another woman who had made false sexual assault allegations against a man. And if that wasn't bad enough, 39.6% of women indicated that they could imagine, if needs be, making a false sexual assault allegation against a man if it were to benefit them. That's disturbing. And this is exactly the kind of data that many in my realm, the men's rights activists of the world, and just men in general who have experienced false accusations, have warned about for decades. I often get criticized for mostly debunking viral claims about men. Well, fair enough. Let's check a claim about women for a change. In this video, the commentator makes two claims. Claim number one. Around 31% of women reported knowing another woman who had made false SA allegations against a man. Claim number two. 39.6% of women indicated that they could imagine, if needs be, making a false SA allegation against a man if it were to benefit them. So, false SA allegations. A very interesting and controversial topic. So, let's check whether there's any validity to these claims. The numbers seem to come from a study called A Lies and Imagined Intent to Lie by Sharon Burge and Cassandra Matthews, published in Current Psychology in 2021. The study surveyed 255 women, college students and community participants, about false assault claims, including whether they had ever made one, whether they knew someone who had, and whether they could imagine making one in the future. So, right away, we can see one of the main limitations of the study. It is too small to be generalized to all women. And, by the way, the authors acknowledged this too. Another limitation is that the authors did not specify the type of assault claimed. So, some participants could have interpreted assault as a physical assault rather than sexual assault. Keeping these limitations in mind, let's look at the results of the study and whether they match the claims made by the original commentator. One result was that out of 255 women, 18, or 7.1%, said they had lied about being assaulted. But only 4 women said the false claim was made to an authority figure. The other 14 said it was made to friends or family. The second result, which relates to the commentator's first claim, was that 78 women, around 31%, reported knowing someone else who had made a false claim. So, the first claim generally matches what was stated in the paper. But you still need to be careful when interpreting it, since those are not verified cases. The authors themselves say this depends on whether participants could accurately report what they had heard. The commentator's second claim, that 39.6% of women indicated that they could imagine, if needs be, making a false sexual assault allegation against a man if it were to benefit them, is much more misleading. The actual question was whether participants could imagine a situation where they would make a false claim, rated on a 0 to 100 scale, from no, I would never do this, to absolutely, I can imagine one. So, even a very low, non-zero answer could be counted as a positive answer. But that is quite different from saying, I would do this. Also, the question was about imagining a situation. The wording, if needs be, or if it were to benefit them, seems to have been added by the commentator, not used by the authors. The paper does discuss possible motives, like fear, revenge, embarrassment, and excitement, but that is not the same as saying that 39.6% of women would weaponize allegations for personal benefit. So, a more careful wording would be something like this. In one small, exploratory survey of 255 women, 39.6% gave some non-zero answer when asked if they could imagine a situation where they might make a false assault claim. That is much less dramatic, but it is also much more accurate. And this is exactly why we need to be careful with studies like this. Yes, false accusations exist, yes, they can destroy lives, and yes, it is important to talk about them, but that doesn't mean we should take a small, exploratory study, remove the limitations, add more aggressive wording, and then use it to imply something about women in general. I criticize this when creators do it to men, so to stay fair, I should criticize it when creators do it to women too. Because the goal should not be to vilify men or women, the goal should be to try to stay as objective as possible.
